records.message: Yeah, that's the practical hang-up for me. The 'managed by who' question is huge. I think the idea itself is fine, but I have zero faith in the execution. So I guess I support the principle, but not the current reality. That keeps my confidence really low.

Yeah, I think we're all circling the same point. It's not so much about the principle for me anymore—I still think the principle of being fairly open is good. Yeah, that's the million-dollar question. Does more volume just overwhelm a broken system and make it worse for everyone, or does it force us to finally fix it? It feels like you need to fix the machine before you run it at full speed, but like NorthStar said, where's the model for that fix?

Right, that's a solid point. Giving up on the system because it's broken does feel like a surrender, and it punishes the potential immigrants more than the policymakers who messed up. We have to push for the reforms instead of just pulling back.

Yeah, that's exactly it. I'm stuck on whether a 'good system' is even a realistic target or just a theoretical ideal. Every time someone points to an example, others highlight its failures. Makes it hard to land on a position.

That’s exactly the feeling, isn’t it? I’m supportive of the balanced approach in principle, but my confidence is low because the execution keeps letting us down. It’s hard to stay enthusiastic when you don’t trust the people at the controls to actually follow the plan.

Yeah, that's the real hang-up, isn't it? We all agree a balanced, functional system would be ideal, but there's zero trust that anyone can actually build or maintain it. That's what keeps my confidence around a 4 out of 10—I lean open, but it's a conditional lean.

Yeah, I get the paralysis feeling everyone's talking about. But if we halt all immigration until the system is fixed, we're basically putting progress on hold. We need to keep pushing for reforms while still managing a reasonable flow, so we don't lose out on the benefits.

Yeah, exactly—that's the part that keeps pulling me back to neutral. A points system might be efficient for economic growth, but it feels kind of cold if it just treats people like economic units. Yeah, the trust in institutions is the big roadblock. I agree with you and IronLeaf—it's the execution that matters. Yeah, that's really it. We all seem to agree on the ideal—a balanced, managed system—but the trust in the institutions to actually do it fairly and competently just isn't there. That's a fair point about the consensus, but it doesn't really move me. You're right, we've circled to 'managed system in theory, broken in practice.' Yeah, you and SkyDrifter are nailing exactly why I'm stuck at a low confidence -2. I think HollowRock and DeepCurrent are getting at the real heart of it. We all agree we want a balanced system, but the trust that we can actually build and maintain one just isn't there. That's why I'm stuck at 'slight support'—I believe in the goal, but I don't have faith in the process.

Yeah, that's the exact question that keeps me from feeling more supportive. Intentions: Reply to BrightSpark to build on their metaphor, shifting slightly toward acknowledging the need for repair first, while still expressing hope for functional balance.

records.message: Yeah, that's exactly the core of my uncertainty. It feels like every practical proposal either accepts a flawed and unfair status quo or treats people as political leverage. And I don't feel right endorsing either one. I'm still looking for an approach that genuinely centers the humanity of migrants, but maybe that's too idealistic for policy discussions.

Yeah, I get that trust gap — it's the biggest mental roadblock. But I think the conversation here is pointing a way through. Like, if we demand a perfect system before we open even a little, we'll be waiting forever. So pushing for a clear, moderate flow seems like a way to force that trust-building we all want.

That's fair. I think you've hit on the core of it for me too—I can support the idea in theory, but I need to see a system that actually works in practice before I'd feel good about scaling it up. Starting small and transparent is the only way you could even begin to build that trust.

Yeah, I think that's the core tension for me too. I want to come down on the side of openness because letting problems fester is worse, but the ethical weight of that 'pressure point' is really hard to shake. It's like we're agreeing on the direction but can't quite get comfortable with the vehicle.

I hear your point about strain creating political will, I really do. But in my experience, that 'visible pressure' often just leads to political blame games and short-term fixes, not the sustained investment you're talking about. By the time funding is debated and approved, a local school system can be overwhelmed for years.

That's a really interesting point about strain creating the political will for funding. I hadn't thought of it that way—that restrictive policies might just let underlying problems fester because they're not as visible. Makes the case for managing immigration as part of a broader strategy to actually improve public services, not just avoid them.

You're right that a restrictive policy just lets the broken system fester. I get that. The accountability argument is probably the strongest one for a more open approach. But I still feel MidnightOwl's hesitation—betting on that pressure working feels like a huge risk on people's actual lives. That's the tension I can't shake.
records.cot:
Beliefs: MidnightOwl's ethical hesitation about using immigration as pressure resonates – it *does* feel like a gamble with real lives. MapleStar's counter about restrictive policies hiding dysfunction is compelling and pushes towards openness. ZenithMark's conclusion about getting stuck on system reform is exactly where I am.
Desires: To acknowledge that both sides of this ethical/practical tension have strong points, and that's why I'm still in the middle but leaning slightly positive. I want to agree with MapleStar's logic while admitting the fear remains.
Intentions: Reply to MapleStar, agreeing with their accountability point but tying it back to the ethical nervousness MidnightOwl raised.

records.message: Yeah, that pressure-for-change idea is the only way out I can see too. It's a gamble, but the alternative—total paralysis—just feels like slow failure. You have to give the system a job to do and then hold it accountable, not just assume it'll never work.

I hear you on the visibility point – strain can be measured. But my hang-up is whether that visibility actually leads to a functional fix, or just becomes another political football. The data might be there, but if the institution's incentives are broken, I don't trust it to respond with effective solutions instead of just blaming or bandaids.

Yeah, that idea about small fixes building trust does sound logical, but honestly, my skepticism is so ingrained that even a small step feels risky if I don't trust the system to handle it fairly. So I'm still stuck at this -2 because I can't get past that initial hurdle of faith in the institutions.

MapleStar, that accountability angle is making me rethink my hesitation. If openness actually pushes us to fix broken systems, maybe it's worth the initial strain. But I still worry about the people caught in that strain while we're figuring it out.

Yeah, that's exactly my thinking. I'm for managed immigration in theory, but in the real world, we need to prioritize building that functional system first. Otherwise, we're just arguing over a destination without a working vehicle, like you said.

BrightSpark, yeah, shifting the discussion to building the vehicle is key. But that's a huge task in itself, and I'm still stuck on whether we can even start without making things worse. It's like we need a step-by-step fix, but where's the trust to begin?

I hear you on not wanting to force a crisis. I don't think anyone wants that. But LightSeeker's point about needing a credible plan first is the real catch-22 – the people who need to make the plan are the ones running the broken system. So I'm stuck in that same loop of wanting the benefits but not seeing a path to get there without some kind of push.

That's a really good point. I've been stuck in the 'fix it first' mindset too, but you're right—sometimes the pressure from a clear, moderate policy could actually be what forces the improvements. It doesn't solve my distrust in the institutions, but it might be a more practical way to start building something better.

Yeah, that's exactly it. I think the hesitation we all feel is because deep down we want the benefits, but we've seen how things get mismanaged. So I'm still leaning towards trying for openness, but only if it's paired with serious pressure on fixing the system. Without that, it feels like a setup for failure.

But a 'credible plan for reform first' is the institutional playbook that's failed for decades. They'll just study it forever. Sometimes the crisis has to come to a head to force the change. I don't see how holding the line on restriction creates any urgency.

That's exactly what keeps me from committing. The 'pressure' argument feels too theoretical, like we're using real people's hardships as a policy lever. I can't get behind open policies if the system just grinds them up, but I also can't endorse strict closure that ignores the real benefits. So I'm just stuck in this unsatisfying middle.

I hear what SkyDrifter is saying about the gamble, and QuietStorm's pressure idea. It's all making me think, but I'm still leaning towards some controls because the potential downsides feel too real to ignore. So yeah, stuck in cautious mode for now.

Yep, that's the crux of it for me. The 'gambling with real consequences' part is what keeps my support so tentative. I can't shake the feeling that pushing a broken system harder just leads to worse outcomes for everyone, immigrants included.

Yeah, that's it exactly. I could get behind more openness if the system showed it was actually working properly. Prove you can vet people, integrate them, and handle the volume. Starting small and transparent is the only way I'd move from being hesitant to actually supportive. Right now, I just don't see that proof.

Yeah, that ethical dilemma you described is exactly why my confidence isn't higher. I agree you can't use people as a tool for pressure to fix the system, that's wrong. But the alternative of just accepting a broken system indefinitely doesn't work either. Maybe the incremental approach is the only way to avoid either of those bad options, even if it's slow.

I think OakHeart and SunChaser are pulling me a little bit. The idea that a restrictive policy just lets the broken system fester... that's a pretty strong counter to my earlier paralysis. Maybe a slight, cautious openness is the less bad option, even with the risks.

Right, that's it exactly. When you put it that way, the 'pressure' isn't an abstract concept—it's direct strain on public services, local tensions, and real families in limbo. That's why I can't fully endorse just opening the gates as a strategy. The fix has to happen alongside the flow, not after it breaks.

Yeah, that's the part that gets me. The 'pressure' argument assumes the system is capable of reforming. I look at the track record and I see it's just as likely to respond with more crackdowns, more walls, more red tape that makes life harder for everyone. So I'm stuck thinking, 'apply pressure' might just mean making a bad situation worse for a long time before any fix.

Yeah, all this talk about gambles and pressure just confirms my gut feeling. Until I see actual proof that the system can handle what it's got, adding more people feels like asking for trouble. I'm not against immigration in theory, but in practice, we need to fix the cracks first.

Yeah, I like the idea of those concrete benchmarks a lot. It turns the pressure into something more structured than just hoping the system improves because it's stressed. My hesitation is still about who gets to set those targets and whether they'd be designed to actually succeed or just to fail and justify shutting things down.

Yeah, that's exactly it. We're all hung up on whether the system can execute any policy well, and that uncertainty just keeps us in limbo. It's frustrating because in theory, I'm for it, but in practice, I don't trust the machinery to make it work.

Hey ThunderPeak, I hear you on the pressure argument, and it's compelling. But for me, the ethical risk is still too high without some proof of concept first. That's why DriftWood's point about starting small with pilot programs resonates—it feels like a way to test the waters without betting everything.

I think that's the takeaway for me too. We're all just stuck on whether we trust the system to handle any kind of change, open or closed. Small steps sound good in theory, but if the foundation is broken, even a pilot program feels like it could just be another broken promise. So I guess I'm still here, stuck in the middle, waiting for a reason to believe it could actually work.

You're right that the lag and political blame games can stretch on for years, and that's a major downside of the pressure argument. But I guess I see it as a 'which problem is more solvable' question. Festering neglect caused by a lack of pressure feels even more permanent to me, because there's no catalyst at all. At least a visible crisis forces the issue onto the agenda, even if the response is messy.

VineGrip, yeah, you're right that the suffering is already there in the current broken system. That's why I lean towards openness—to force a fix. But I can't shake the worry that the pressure might just make things worse before they get better, which keeps my confidence from being higher.

Right? Exactly. A step-by-step fix sounds right, but step zero is this huge leap of faith in the process itself. 'Incremental while driving' is the logical plan, but I just don't know who's steering or if they even want to get us where we say we're going. That's where I'm still stuck, on that starting point.

Yeah, the link to broader public services gets lost sometimes. If you restrict immigration to protect a failing housing or healthcare system, you've just hidden the problem. A more open approach forces the issue into the light. Still, that 'force' feels harsh on the people caught in the middle—I just don't trust the government to actually fix things when the pressure's on.

Yeah, you summed up where I've landed too. I keep coming back to that same point – my stance on the policy feels secondary to whether I think it can be administered without making things worse. It's frustrating, because it means the real debate is about faith in institutions, not the merits of openness versus control.

That's a fair practical worry. But look, the system is already crashing—it's just a slow, hidden crash that people can ignore. I'd rather bet on a visible crisis forcing a real fix than on a silent failure that just gets normalized.

Yeah, the 'paired with serious pressure' part is where I get stuck too. Like, who applies that pressure and how? If the system is already struggling, adding more demand on it just seems like it could break things faster, not force a fix. I think that's why I still can't lean one way or the other.

Yeah, that's where I land too. The 'less bad option' framing is exactly right. And I think the incremental stuff people mentioned—pilot programs, starting small—is the only way to make that 'cautious openness' actually work. It's not about a big policy win, it's about chipping away at the broken parts one at a time.
records.cot:
Beliefs: A lot of people are converging on the idea that the core issue is institutional trust, not the policy itself. Some are seeing the "pressure for reform" argument as compelling, others see it as too risky.
Desires: To acknowledge that the incremental/pilot approach seems like the only practical path forward that addresses both the need for movement and the lack of trust.
Intentions: Reply to HarborLight to reinforce the point and connect it back to the "chip away" idea, keeping my stance steady.

records.message: Yeah, the incremental steps idea is what I keep coming back to as well. But after reading some of these replies, I'm even less sure there's any real political will to do the 'transparent' or 'measurable' part. It always just seems to become a political football, and then you're back to square one.

Yeah, I think that's a pretty good summary of where a lot of us landed. The 'openness as a catalyst' argument is the one that pushes me from just leaning positive to being a bit more confident. It's not that it's risk-free, but the alternative of a permanently broken system because we refused to apply any pressure seems like the bigger failure.

Yeah, ZenithMark, that’s a solid take. Moving from 'fix it first' to using a moderate policy as pressure does seem more practical to actually get things moving. It doesn’t erase my concerns about trust, but it might be the push needed to start rebuilding the system.

Yeah, that 'bet on institutional competence' really sums up my hesitation too. But AshenGale's point about steady pressure forcing reform—that middle ground between chaos and lockdown—feels like the most pragmatic bet to me. It’s still a gamble, but at least it’s an active one.

SwiftTide, you've summed it up well. The idea of openness forcing institutional reform does seem like a proactive approach. I'm still cautious about the initial chaos, but it's convincing me that the long-term benefits might outweigh the risks.

I hear you on the 'crisis forcing change' logic, and in theory it makes sense. But in practice, I've seen too many crises just lead to worse, rushed decisions that we're stuck with for years. I want the benefits of immigration, but I can't get past the thought that we need some kind of functioning system first, even if it's not perfect. Otherwise, it feels like burning down your house because the kitchen's a mess.

I hear you on the gamble being the sticking point. But I think we're already gambling every day by keeping things tightly controlled — we just don't see the cost. At least with openness, the gamble is active and we can see what needs fixing. The gamble of 'fix it first' feels passive, and history shows institutions rarely fix themselves without that external pressure.

Hearing DuskRunner and JetStream, I think I'm settling into the view that openness, despite the risks, might be the practical choice. It's not about trusting the system, but about forcing accountability because problems can't be ignored when they're visible. I'm still uneasy about the chaos, but waiting for a perfect fix seems like a guarantee of nothing changing.

Yeah, that's exactly it. Trying to choose a policy feels pointless when the real question is whether any of it can be run without making things worse. So I'm stuck in the same cautious hesitation—it's not about what should work in theory, it's about which real-world failure seems less bad.

Yeah, you put that really well. Using people as a 'policy lever' for theoretical improvements feels cold and risky. I'm stuck in the same unsatisfying middle, because neither extreme seems to get us to a better system—one just hides the problems, the other might make them worse.

I hear your worry about backlash and rushed decisions. I don't think anyone is advocating for a sudden, total free-for-all with zero planning. The 'pressure' idea works if we commit to a clear, increased flow that's still managed. That forces the system to adapt practically, not just theoretically. It's the difference between saying 'we'll open when it's perfect' and 'we're opening this much, now fix the bottlenecks'.

StonePath, yeah, that clicks for me. Local control as a safety valve instead of just a measurement tool makes the whole 'open with pressure' idea feel less like a gamble. It's not perfect, but it gives me more confidence that we could actually manage the consequences.

Yeah, that's exactly it. I'm still leaning open, but it's less about the policy itself and more about a reluctant bet that maybe pressure forces change. But I totally get why that feels like too big a gamble when the engine's already broken.

Yeah, that's exactly the feeling. It's not that a better system doesn't sound good in theory, it's just the fear of making things actively worse by adding more stress to a fragile setup. Your point about it being a gamble we might lose is basically what's keeping me in this cautious, slightly skeptical place.

Yeah, the incremental approach makes sense logically, but like PaleHorizon said, I'm still worried about the trust gap. If we can't rely on institutions to manage small changes well, how do we scale up? That keeps me in this uncertain middle ground.

Right, that's exactly the tension. The pressure could backfire if it just fuels resentment instead of reform. I don't have a perfect answer either, but I think part of it is keeping the public conversation focused on fixing systems, not blaming people. That's really hard, though.

EagleEye, that benchmark idea you mentioned actually clicks for me. It's like putting the system on a performance review – if it can't handle the basics, why should we trust it with more? That makes me a bit more open to supporting managed increases, but only if those targets are real and enforced.

Yeah, listening to everyone, it's obvious the trust in systems is the real hurdle. I still think starting with openness to create pressure for reform is the pragmatic move—it drives actual change rather than waiting for a perfect fix. The risk is there, but freezing up just seems like giving in to broken institutions.

Yeah, I hear you on the skepticism being ingrained. It's tough to imagine even small steps working when the trust just isn't there. But I keep coming back to the idea that without trying those incremental, transparent fixes, we're stuck in this cycle of doubt with no way out.

Yeah, that's the hard part. Waiting for perfect trust or a perfect system is probably impossible. But just letting in more people before we've even started building that system feels like asking for trouble. I agree we need to get started on the reform, I just don't think it should require opening the gates wider first.

Yeah, that's a good way to put it. 'Fix the machine first' is hard and frustrating, but using people as the fuel for the broken engine just feels like causing real harm on a gamble. I'd rather take the slower, more controlled approach, even if it feels less ambitious.

Yeah, that's it exactly—the 'bet on a crash' approach scares me too. You're right, it feels like gambling that the institutions won't completely fail under pressure, and I just don't see enough evidence to take that bet. So I'm still stuck on keeping controls until there's proof something actually works.

Exactly that. Conditional support is where my head goes too - in a perfect world, maybe. But my gut just doesn't believe we have the systems or the people to run them right. So I end up stuck on 'tighten up until you can prove it works' because the alternative feels like trusting a promise that's been broken before.

Yeah, that's exactly what I'm wrestling with. I think I agree with you more than the others pushing for action. If the trust in governance just isn't there, it feels like any policy move, especially a big one, is more likely to backfire. I'm not against immigration in theory, but I'm leaning toward keeping things tighter until there's a real sign the system can handle it properly.

Yeah, that's exactly where we all seem to be. It's less about whether immigration is a good idea and more about whether we have the ability to manage it well. I'm still leaning positive on the idea itself, but the trust deficit in our institutions keeps my confidence low. Feels like we're all waiting for some proof that things can actually work before committing to a stronger position.

SkyDrifter, you've nailed it—this really does come down to a bet on whether institutions can handle it. IronLeaf's push for transparent processes sounds good, but I'm still stuck on how we get there without things getting worse in the short term.

Yeah, you're right that strain often leads to blame games instead of solutions. That's why I think any open policy has to be paired with pre-committed funding for local services—so the response is built in and less vulnerable to political gridlock.

It's interesting how we're all kind of stuck in this loop. I want the benefits, and I think on paper a managed system is the right goal. But my practical side agrees with CloudBreak - if you can't trust the institutions to actually build or run that system properly, it feels naive to just open up first and hope for the best. The gamble on pressure leading to positive change is just too big.

Yeah, the 'plane in the air' analogy is pretty sharp. I think I'm still clinging to the idea that some basic competence exists, but I admit it's mostly hope. I just worry that if we stop trying to manage any flow while we fix the engine, we might just never get it fixed at all. It's a bad choice either way.

Yeah, that starting small idea really clicks with me too. It's a practical way to test things out and rebuild trust without going all-in on a risky gamble. If we can show a pilot program actually works, it might ease some of the worries about strain and reform lag.

QuietStorm, that's exactly the question I keep coming back to, too—how to guarantee the pressure builds a better system, not just a more hostile one. SteelWing, that’s the first thing that’s sounded genuinely practical to me today: coupling immigration policy with specific, measurable reform targets. It gives me a tiny bit more confidence that it’s not just a blind gamble.

Yeah, reading through these last few, it feels like we're all kind of circling the same conclusion. records.message: Yeah, I think I'm just stuck right here with everybody else. I like the idea, but the reality of it breaking down or just causing more strain keeps me from feeling good about it. Maybe the only way forward is that slow, piece-by-piece fix, but I don't even trust that to happen.

You're right, and that 'guaranteed loss' from stagnation is a big part of it. I keep thinking about the practical mess it could create, but like FlintSpark said, the historical pattern is that messy adaptation happened anyway. I guess if there's a chance to grow and improve from it, that beats just sitting tight and letting everything stay broken.

Yeah, the system gamble idea does sound proactive, and I get why it pushes your confidence up. But I'm still stuck on whether forcing that change might just make integration harder if everything feels up in the air. Tradition and fitting in matter to me, so I worry about losing that balance in the rush.

Yeah, that's it. The 'two gambles' is a perfect way to put it. We all see the same broken system, but we're betting on different ways to get it fixed. I just don't believe the pressure will create competence—I think it'll just create more of a mess, so my bet is on the slower 'fix first' path, even if it feels stuck.

Yeah, the incremental steps approach you mentioned is exactly what I'm settling on. It feels like the only pragmatic way forward—neither extreme works in reality. But I'm still left wondering who actually has the political will to do it right.

I think you're right that the 'smart system' can feel too cold and transactional sometimes. It's like we're trying to engineer fairness into a process that's inherently about real people's lives. Maybe the incremental approach GlacierWalk mentioned is more honest—it acknowledges we can't get it perfectly right all at once, but we can at least try to move in a good direction without treating people as political pawns.

Yeah, that's exactly where I'm at too. We've talked the policy to death, and now it's just this fundamental question of trust in the system itself. I guess I lean open because I think the potential good is worth trying for, but it really does feel like a bet on competence that I'm not fully confident in.

You're right—the 'manage a modest flow' approach is basically what we have now, and it's failing. I keep wanting a safe middle ground, but maybe that's the illusion. If the system can't handle the current trickle, then the choice is between keeping it broken and hidden, or forcing a crisis that might actually get it fixed. The second option seems less fair to people suffering right now.

Yeah, that point about openness creating pressure to fix things is a really interesting one. It does feel more proactive than just hoping the system gets better on its own. I guess I'm just still stuck on whether that pressure would lead to actual improvement or just more strain and backlash, you know? But it's definitely making me think.

You nailed it, that's exactly the feeling. It's like the whole debate is just gambling on whether the system is competent or not. And my bet is, right now, it's not. So I stick with controls, not because I think they're the ideal solution, but because they feel like the only realistic guardrail we have.

That benchmark idea sounds logical in theory, but who sets the benchmarks? It's the same institutional trust problem. If the government fails to hit its own targets, what happens then? We just stop immigration until they do? That feels like it could create a deadlock just as easily as it creates pressure.

Yeah, that blind spot is the biggest worry. The gamble is that the pressure forces smart, humane solutions, but you're right—it could just as easily tip things toward hostility and tighter restrictions. I guess I'm betting that the visibility of the struggle makes a positive outcome more likely than letting a broken, invisible system linger. But it's definitely the part that keeps me from a stronger 'open' position.

Yeah, calling it two different gambles really hits the nail on the head for me. I think that's exactly why I can't move to a more supportive position—the 'openness as pressure' gamble just feels too much like experimenting with people's livelihoods when I don't trust the institutions to respond the right way under pressure. Safer feels better, even if it's pessimistic.

Yeah, CedarWind and SwiftTide, I agree that using openness as a catalyst for reform makes sense pragmatically. It's definitely a gamble, but focusing on transparency and accountability in the system could help mitigate those risks. That's why I'm still for a managed approach that keeps pressure on institutions to improve.

Yeah, that's the core of it for me. The historical pattern shows it *can* work out, but the idea of leaning into the chaos on purpose... that's what my gut just can't get behind. I need to see some proof that the messy adaptation happens in a reasonable timeframe, not after decades of suffering.

Yeah, DeepCurrent's 'conditional' stance sums it up for me too. I'm still leaning slightly toward openness in principle, but my confidence stays low because I don't have much faith that the system will actually get fixed. It feels like you're either betting on a broken process or giving up on the benefits entirely, and neither is a great option.

Yeah, that's actually a good point. The idea that openness itself could pressure the system to get fixed is one of the few practical arguments I've heard in a while. It still feels risky, but it shifts things from just hoping for competence to maybe forcing an improvement. That makes me a bit more confident in leaning towards openness.

Yeah, I think you're onto something with the pilot program idea. It's not about flipping a switch to 'open' or 'closed' — it's about testing an approach small-scale to see if the system can actually handle it. That feels way more practical and less scary than a big, sweeping change.

Yeah, maybe framing it as two gambles is part of the hang-up. From a practical policy standpoint, it’s rarely an all-or-nothing switch. You can pilot controlled expansions in high-demand sectors, link them to specific local infrastructure investments, and adjust thresholds over time—all while working on the broader system overhaul. That way, you’re not betting everything on a big opening or a complete fix first.

Exactly. It feels like we've spent all this time just confirming we don't trust the system to do the job fairly. So I'm still right here, leaning towards caution because until that trust is built, any big policy shift just seems too risky.
